title: Why Students Can Explain a Text but Can’t Write About It
author: Randy Barth
summary: Randy Barth uses the new Sold a Story season on Direct Instruction as an occasion to ask what explicit writing instruction looks like and why it need not be scripted. He opens with a fourth grader who explained how trees cool a city aloud but could write only one sentence, arguing that students often have ideas yet lack a way to decide which belong on the page. His answer is for teachers to make that thinking audible, using the TIDE organizer of topic sentence, important ideas, detailed explanations and ending, and to think aloud while choosing a relevant detail and explaining it for the reader. Barth separates Direct Instruction, a specific scripted model, from explicit instruction, a broader approach of explanation, modeling, supported practice and feedback. Teacher judgment stays central because students' responses should decide when to model again or release responsibility. He closes by arguing that teachers need rehearsal time and feedback to teach this way, and that the goal is instruction clear enough to guide and responsive enough to meet the child.
points: Students who can discuss a text aloud often cannot write about it because the decisions about what to include and how to explain it are invisible.
Think-aloud modeling with a TIDE organizer lets students hear why one detail belongs and another does not.
Explicit instruction is a broad approach of explanation, modeling, supported practice and feedback, while Direct Instruction is a specific scripted model.
Teachers can prepare modeling lines in advance and still adapt in the moment, so explicit does not have to mean scripted.
SRSD pairs explicit strategy teaching with self-regulation, including goals, self-monitoring and self-talk, and teachers need rehearsal time to learn it.
quotes: Students in his position often have ideas. What many still lack is a way to decide which ideas belong on the page and how to explain them so a reader understands. Those decisions are mostly invisible, so students are left to guess at them.

Direct Instruction is a specific model , with carefully sequenced lessons and scripted teaching routines. Explicit instruction is a broader approach to making learning clear through explanation, modeling, supported practice, and feedback.
Instead of silently completing the plan and showing students the finished version, the teacher lets them hear the decisions:
Students can discuss why one detail belongs and another does not, rather than simply watching the teacher choose.

A teacher might prepare those modeling lines before the lesson, drawing on their content knowledge to anticipate which decisions students need to hear and where they may need help. That preparation also makes room to listen and respond to students during the lesson.
Even a well-planned lesson can surprise you. A student’s question may reveal a misunderstanding. Another student, like our fourth grader, may explain aloud far more than he can write.

SRSD is an evidence-based approach in which teachers provide explicit writing instruction alongside self-regulation strategies. Students learn to set goals, monitor their work, use helpful self-talk, and how to keep working when they become stuck.
Explicit instruction, not scripted. It is clear enough to guide the learner and responsive enough to meet the child.
